blocks.text: A lumbar puncture (LP) needle is a specialized needle used to enter the subarachnoid space in the lower lumbar spine to obtain cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), measure CSF opening pressure when indicated, or administer specific intrathecal medications.

In a Medicine and Pediatrics OSCE, you must know the instrument, relevant spinal anatomy, indications and contraindications for the procedure, CSF collection, complications, and special safety considerations in children.

Critical clinical principle: A lumbar puncture is not performed simply because meningitis is suspected. The patient must first be assessed for contraindications and features requiring stabilization or further investigation.
Name: Lumbar puncture needle, also called a spinal needle.
Classification: Specialized sterile needle for access to the spinal subarachnoid space.
Common types: Cutting-bevel needles, such as Quincke, and atraumatic pencil-point needles, such as Whitacre and Sprotte.
Typical components: Needle shaft, hub, stylet and, in some sets, an introducer.
Common uses: CSF sampling, CSF pressure measurement and selected intrathecal procedures.
Has a sharp cutting bevel. It is a traditional spinal needle design and may be used for diagnostic lumbar puncture.
Has a pencil-point tip with a lateral opening. It separates tissue fibres rather than cutting them in the same way as a conventional cutting-bevel needle.
Another atraumatic spinal needle design with a pencil-point tip and side opening.

Atraumatic needles are generally preferred for many diagnostic lumbar punctures when suitable equipment and trained operators are available, because they reduce the risk of post-dural-puncture headache.
Suspected meningitis: To examine CSF for evidence of infection when lumbar puncture is safe and appropriate.
Suspected encephalitis: To investigate CNS infection, alongside other investigations.
Suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage: In selected patients when further investigation is indicated after initial assessment and imaging.
Inflammatory or demyelinating disease: For example, selected investigations in suspected multiple sclerosis.
Selected neurological disorders: When CSF analysis may clarify the diagnosis.
Measurement of CSF opening pressure in appropriate circumstances.
Intrathecal administration of selected medications by trained clinicians using appropriate equipment.
Other specialist procedures involving the spinal CSF space.

High-yield OSCE point: Lumbar puncture is not the same as spinal anaesthesia, although both involve access to the spinal region. The needle, technique, purpose and medication-safety requirements differ.
The hollow metal shaft that passes through the tissues toward the subarachnoid space. Its length and gauge must be appropriate for the patient and procedure.
A removable solid insert that occupies the needle lumen during insertion. It helps prevent tissue coring and blockage. It is removed when checking for CSF flow, according to the procedural technique.
The proximal part of the needle used for handling and, where appropriate, connection to a compatible device.
A short guide needle that helps the spinal needle pass through superficial tissues and reduces bending, particularly when using fine-gauge needles.
The tip design determines how the needle passes through tissue. Atraumatic needles have a rounded tip with a side opening rather than the cutting bevel of a Quincke needle.
Provides access to CSF for diagnostic investigations.
Enables direct measurement of CSF opening pressure when indicated and measured correctly.
Helps investigate important neurological and infectious conditions.
Specialized needle designs permit procedures in appropriately selected patients.
Atraumatic needle designs reduce post-dural-puncture headache compared with conventional cutting-bevel needles in many settings.
A properly selected needle allows controlled CSF collection by a trained operator.
Requires trained personnel and strict aseptic technique.
May be technically difficult in obesity, spinal deformity or uncooperative patients.
CSF results may be difficult to interpret after a traumatic tap.
A normal initial CSF result does not exclude every neurological or infectious condition.
LP can delay treatment if clinicians pursue it despite instability or contraindications.
Cutting-bevel needles have a higher risk of post-dural-puncture headache than atraumatic needles.
LP does not replace blood cultures, imaging or other investigations when these are indicated.
Before lumbar puncture, the clinician must assess the patient, establish the indication and consider whether the procedure is safe.
Appropriate sterile spinal needle with stylet.
Introducer, if required.
Sterile gloves, antiseptic and sterile drapes.
Local anaesthetic and appropriate injection equipment.
Sterile CSF collection tubes, correctly labelled.
Manometer and compatible connections when opening pressure measurement is required.
Dressing and sharps container.
Appropriate monitoring and resuscitation equipment for the clinical setting.
Confirm patient identity, indication and consent; use an appropriate guardian consent process for children.
Assess vital signs, airway, breathing, circulation and neurological status.
Look for signs suggesting a space-occupying lesion or raised intracranial pressure.
Assess for bleeding risk, anticoagulant use, platelet abnormalities and coagulation disorders.
Inspect the proposed insertion site for infection or skin lesions.
Review previous spinal surgery, spinal abnormalities and relevant imaging where indicated.
Ensure the appropriate operator, equipment and assistance are available.
Explain positioning, expected sensations and possible complications.
Use strict aseptic technique throughout the procedure.

content_groups.group_title: When should lumbar puncture be deferred?

blocks.text: Do not proceed until the patient has been appropriately assessed if there is:
Haemodynamic or respiratory instability.
Significant concern for an intracranial mass lesion or dangerous pressure gradient.
Local infection at the proposed puncture site.
A significant bleeding risk or uncorrected relevant coagulopathy.
Another patient-specific contraindication requiring specialist assessment.

Important: Suspected meningitis may be a medical emergency. If lumbar puncture is unsafe or would delay urgent treatment, obtain appropriate cultures when feasible and start indicated empiric treatment without waiting for LP.

subsections.subsection_title: How to perform a lumbar puncture — step-by-step OSCE demonstration

blocks.text: The following is a clinical examination framework. Actual insertion should be performed only by appropriately trained clinicians under supervision where required.
The patient may sit leaning forward or lie in the lateral decubitus position with the back flexed. Choose the position according to clinical needs and whether opening pressure must be measured.
Identify the iliac crests and estimate the L4 vertebral level. The usual insertion region is the L3–L4 or L4–L5 interspace, below the termination of the spinal cord in most adults.
Perform hand hygiene, use appropriate sterile PPE, clean the site with the recommended antiseptic and allow it to dry, then apply sterile drapes.
Infiltrate the appropriate skin and deeper tissues with local anaesthetic, after checking allergies and the intended dose.

The trained operator advances the needle through the selected interspace using the appropriate anatomical orientation and technique. The stylet is handled according to the needle design and procedural protocol.

Once the subarachnoid space is reached, CSF flow is assessed. If opening pressure is required, it should be measured using a compatible manometer in the appropriate position before substantial CSF removal.
Collect the required volume into correctly labelled sterile tubes according to the requested tests and laboratory protocol. Avoid unnecessary collection, particularly in neonates and small children.
Replace the stylet as recommended for the needle and technique, withdraw the needle safely and apply a dressing. Dispose of sharps appropriately.
Reassess the patient, document the procedure and any complications, and send the specimens promptly with the relevant clinical information.
The important anatomical structures include:
Skin and subcutaneous tissue.
Supraspinous and interspinous ligaments.
Ligamentum flavum.
Epidural space.
Dura mater.
Arachnoid mater.
Subarachnoid space containing CSF and cauda equina nerve roots.
The adult spinal cord usually terminates around L1–L2, although there is individual variation. Lumbar puncture is therefore usually performed below this level.
The number of tubes, their order and the volume required depend on the clinical question and laboratory policy.

blocks.text: CSF should be transported promptly, especially when bacterial meningitis is suspected. Do not delay time-critical treatment while arranging specimen collection.
Lumbar puncture requires individualized assessment. Important concerns include:
Suspected intracranial mass effect or a dangerous pressure gradient.
Uncorrected significant bleeding risk.
Infection at the insertion site.
Cardiopulmonary instability.
Certain spinal abnormalities or anatomical difficulties.
A raised opening pressure alone is not an automatic contraindication in every patient. The underlying cause, neurological findings and risk of a pressure gradient determine whether LP is appropriate.
Often worse when sitting or standing and relieved by lying down. Atraumatic needles reduce the risk.

items: 2. Transient back pain or radicular symptoms

blocks.text: Local discomfort or brief shooting pain can occur. Persistent neurological symptoms require urgent assessment.
Blood enters the CSF specimen during needle insertion, complicating interpretation of red cells and other findings.
Rare but potentially serious, particularly when bleeding risk is increased.
Aseptic technique is essential to minimize the risk of introducing infection.
A major rare complication in a patient with dangerous intracranial mass effect is cerebral herniation. This is why clinical assessment and appropriate investigation before LP are essential.
Aftercare: Routine prolonged bed rest has not been shown to prevent post-dural-puncture headache. Provide appropriate monitoring, advice and management based on symptoms and clinical circumstances.
The needle itself is not a diagnostic instrument. The clinician assesses CSF appearance, opening pressure where measured, laboratory results and the patient's condition.
Clear CSF.
Opening pressure within the appropriate reference range for the patient's age and measurement conditions.
Cell count, protein, glucose and microbiology consistent with the clinical context.
Cloudy or purulent-appearing CSF.
Blood-stained CSF.
Raised or unexpectedly low opening pressure.
Increased white-cell count or protein.
Low CSF glucose relative to paired blood glucose.
Positive Gram stain, culture or molecular test.
No single CSF appearance or result reliably excludes meningitis. Interpretation depends on the full clinical picture, age, timing, prior treatment and other investigations.
Lumbar puncture in children requires particular attention to positioning, physiological stability, needle selection and specimen volume.
Neonates and infants: CSF reference ranges differ from those of older children and adults. Interpret results using age-appropriate standards.
Needle selection: Choose an appropriate length and gauge for the child's size and the procedure. Use an atraumatic needle where suitable and available.
Positioning: Flex the spine gently without compromising breathing. Excessive neck flexion in a small infant can obstruct the airway.
Respiratory monitoring: Observe breathing, oxygenation and overall stability, particularly in young infants.
Blood volume and CSF volume: Collect only the amount required for the investigations. Avoid unnecessary repeated procedures.
Consent and comfort: Explain the procedure to the caregiver, obtain appropriate consent and use age-appropriate comfort measures.
Sedation: If required, it should be administered under an appropriate protocol with suitable monitoring and airway support.
Meningitis: In a seriously ill child, stabilization and prompt antimicrobial treatment take priority over performing an unsafe or delayed lumbar puncture.
Traumatic tap: Blood contamination may complicate CSF interpretation. Do not rely on a simple correction formula alone to exclude meningitis.
Post-procedure observation: Monitor for deterioration, persistent pain, neurological symptoms and other complications.

High-yield pediatric warning: A bulging fontanelle in an infant requires clinical assessment but is not, by itself, an absolute contraindication to lumbar puncture. The full neurological and physiological assessment determines safety.
Remember the usual lumbar puncture interspaces.
These are below the usual termination of the spinal cord in adults.
Stability — assess the patient and stabilize first.
Assess contraindications — especially mass effect and bleeding risk.
Find the landmarks — identify the appropriate lumbar interspace.
Ensure asepsis — prepare, collect and label specimens correctly.
Lateral decubitus — a suitable position for opening pressure measurement when clinically appropriate.
Post-procedure monitoring — assess the patient and recognize complications.

subsections.subsection_title: Common OSCE questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. Identify this instrument.
This is a lumbar puncture needle, used to access the subarachnoid space in the lumbar spine for CSF sampling, pressure measurement or selected intrathecal procedures.
Q2. What is the difference between a Quincke and a Whitacre needle?
A Quincke needle has a cutting bevel, whereas a Whitacre needle has an atraumatic pencil-point design with a lateral aperture.
Q3. At which level is lumbar puncture usually performed?
At the L3–L4 or L4–L5 interspace in adults, below the usual termination of the spinal cord.
Q4. What is the purpose of the stylet?
It occupies the needle lumen during insertion, helping prevent tissue coring and blockage. Its handling follows the needle design and procedural technique.
Q5. Why is an atraumatic needle preferred?
It reduces the risk of post-dural-puncture headache compared with conventional cutting-bevel needles in many settings.
Q6. What are the major contraindications to lumbar puncture?
Important concerns include suspected dangerous intracranial mass effect, significant uncorrected bleeding risk, infection at the puncture site and cardiopulmonary instability.
Q7. What is a traumatic tap?
Blood enters the CSF specimen because of vessel injury during needle insertion, potentially complicating interpretation of the results.
Q8. In what position should opening pressure be measured?
Generally in the lateral decubitus position, with appropriate relaxation and correct manometer positioning, when clinically feasible and according to the measurement protocol.
Q9. What should you do if a child with suspected meningitis is unstable?
Stabilize the child and initiate urgent indicated treatment. Defer lumbar puncture until it is safe; do not delay time-critical antimicrobial treatment while waiting for the procedure.
Q10. Does a normal-looking CSF exclude meningitis?
No. CSF appearance alone cannot exclude meningitis. Laboratory findings must be interpreted alongside the clinical presentation and other investigations.
Common mistakes include:
Failing to check for contraindications before the procedure.
Confusing the lumbar puncture needle with an epidural needle.
Incorrectly identifying the lumbar interspace.
Forgetting that the spinal cord usually ends above the usual adult puncture site.
Failing to maintain strict aseptic technique.
Measuring opening pressure in an inappropriate position or after substantial CSF removal.
Collecting or labelling CSF tubes incorrectly.
Assuming that clear CSF excludes meningitis.
Delaying antibiotics in a seriously ill patient because LP has not yet been performed.
Assuming that every bulging fontanelle is an absolute contraindication.

Examiner's tip: Structure your answer as instrument identification → indications → anatomy → contraindications → equipment → procedure → complications. This demonstrates safe clinical reasoning, not just instrument recognition.
A 6-year-old child presents with fever, headache, neck stiffness and suspected meningitis. You are shown a spinal needle and asked to discuss lumbar puncture.
Identify the instrument and name two types.
State the usual lumbar puncture levels.
Name four investigations performed on CSF.
State four important contraindications or reasons to defer the procedure.
Explain the difference between a Quincke and an atraumatic needle.
Describe your immediate priorities if the child is unstable.
